evidence: Cic. Fat. 1: sed decet augentem linguam Latīnam nōmināre mōrālem (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Cicero made the word for Greek ἠθικός (Fat. 1), and Seneca and Quintilian took it up, mostly of the part of philosophy that deals with conduct. In plain speech Latin more often says dē mōribus, or names the duty in question (officium).

evidence: Cic. Fat. 1: nōs eam partem philosophiae dē mōribus appellāre solēmus (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: The plain Latin: a moral question is a question about conduct (see morals).

phrases.latin: quia pertinet ad mōrēs, quōs ἤθη Graecī vocant, nōs eam partem philosophiae dē mōribus appellāre solēmus; sed decet augentem linguam Latīnam nōmināre mōrālem
phrases.english: because it concerns conduct, which the Greeks call ēthē, we usually call that part of philosophy “on conduct”; but in enriching the Latin language it is fitting to call it “moral”

phrases.latin: philosophiae trēs partēs esse dīxērunt, mōrālem, nātūrālem, et ratiōnālem
phrases.english: they said that philosophy has three parts, the moral, the natural and the rational

sources: Lewis & Short: moralis · Lewis & Short: mos
Quotations marked “Lewis & Short” are given as Lewis & Short cites them, with its references, in the house spelling (macrons, consonantal j); they have not been checked against a modern edition.
